name: Ewa Krempa-Czuchryta
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 11184/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mrs Ewa Krempa-Czuchryta. The applicant was not legally represented. The Polish Government (’the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The fourth expert's report in the case was submitted in September 1997. It was served on the applicant's lawyer on 27 January 1998. On 24 February 1998 the applicant appealed. On 13 March 2001 the Supreme Court refused to entertain the cassation appeal as no important legal issue arose in theCase. the so-called “institute opinion’ (opinia instytucjonalna) (opina instytUCJonalna).

name: Ali Riza Göktan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33402/96) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Mr Ali Riza Göktan alleged a violation of Article 6 of the Convention. The applicant consistently protested his innocence, saying that he had been the victim of a put-up job by customs officers. By a decision of 27 November 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government, but not the applicant, filed written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) and this case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The applicant was charged with drug trafficking and detained in March 1991. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment for the criminal offences of importing, purchasing, possessing and transporting drugs. The applicant was also ordered to pay a customs fine of FRF 400,000 that was imposed jointly and severally for the customs offence of illegally importing goods. On 27 June 1991 the public prosecutor sought an order for two years' prison in default, as the customs fine had not been paid. He made an urgent application to the President of the Mulhouse tribunal de grande instance, arguing that the Customs Office had failed to serve him with a demand for payment. However, he later withdrew his appeal and the case was struck out of the Court of Cassation's list. Customs law is a special branch of law and an exception to the general law. Appeal upheld that order for the following reasons: “Under Article 388 of the Customs Code the court may make an express order for a person who has been convicted of a [customs] offence or offence relating to indirect taxation to remain in custody, even if an ordinary appeal or appeal on points of law has been lodged” The Court of Cassation ruled that the applicant's appeal against that decision had lapsed, as he had not lodged written pleadings in support of his appeal within the statutory time-limit. He alleged a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention, and of Article 6 of the Convention. Ali Göktan was found guilty of an offence under the drug-trafficking and customs-offences legislation. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment and a customs fine. He made an application for a ruling that that term should run concurrently with the prison sentence. The Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal for the following reasons. Code, which required sentences to run concurrently, had not been infringed by the trial court and could not enable a prison sentence and term of imprisonment in default to be served concurrently. The applicant, who has now completed all the sentences he was required to serve, was deported to Turkey, where he came from.

Case originated in an application (no. 33402/96) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and of Article 4 of Protocol No. 11. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 27 November 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government, but not the applicant, filed written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52§ 1) The applicant was charged with drug trafficking and detained in March 1991. On 3 June 1991 he was brought before the Strasbourg Criminal Court. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment for the criminal offences of importing, purchasing, possessing and transporting drugs. He also had to pay a customs fine of FRF 400,000 that was imposed jointly and severally for the customs offence of illegally importing goods. On 4 September 1994 the applicant completed his prison sentence. However, he remained in custody pursuant to the order requiring him to serve two years’ imprisonment in default of payment of the customs fine. He later withdrew his appeal and the case was struck out of the Court of Cassation’s list on 3 February 1992. The courts have consistently held that customs law is a special branch of law and an exception to the general law. Appeal upheld that order for the following reasons: “Under Article 388 of the Customs Code the court may make an express order for a person who has been convicted of a [customs] offence or offence relating to indirect taxation to remain in custody, even if an ordinary appeal or appeal on points of law has been lodged, until he or she has paid the fiscal penalties imposed on him or her” The applicant alleged a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention, which sets out the non bis in idem rule, and of Article 6 of the Convention. Ali Göktan was found guilty of an offence under the drug-trafficking and customs-offences legislation. After being ordered to serve two years' imprisonment in default of payment, he made an application for a ruling that that term should run concurrently with the prison sentence. In a judgment of 16 September 1997 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal for the following reasons. Code, which required sentences to run concurrently, had not been infringed by the trial court and could not enable a prison sentence to be served concurrently. The applicant, who has now completed all the sentences he was required to serve, was deported to Turkey, where he came from, pursuant to the permanent exclusion order.

name: Eser Ceylan
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant claims to have been insulted and beaten, in particular, hit with truncheons on the legs, and that one of the policemen sexually harassed her. The same police officer punched the applicant in her right eye after she had been placed in the police vehicle. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant was charged with taking part in an unauthorised demonstration. A forensic expert noted that there were no traces of battery on the applicant's body other than those mentioned in the report of 12 December 2000. On 30 January 2001 the public prosecutor decided not to prosecute the police officers who had been on duty at the relevant time. The judge of the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance sent a letter to the Ankara public prosecutor's office, stating that almost all of the defendants in the case had complained of ill-treatment by the security forces. He concluded that there was no concrete evidence other than the complainants' allegations of an “abstract nature” The Ministry of the Interior lodged an action for compensation against the applicant and the other co-accused. The court's reasoned decision refers to evidence such as eye-witness reports, video recordings of the Security Directorate. According to the information available in the file, the compensation proceedings were apparently still pending on the date on which the present judgment was adopted. On 22 January 2004 the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance acquitted the applicant on account of lack of evidence. The application was dismissed on 6 July 2001 by the Kırıkkale Assize Court. The case was referred to the closest assize court, against the decision of 30 January 2001.

The case originated in an application (no. 14166/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant claims to have been insulted and beaten, in particular, hit with truncheons on the legs, and that one of the policemen sexually harassed her. The same police officer punched the applicant in her right eye after she had been placed in the police vehicle. A forensic expert found no traces of battery on the applicant's body other than those mentioned in the report of 12 December 2000. The public prosecutor decided not to prosecute the police officers who had been on duty at the relevant time. The judge of the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance sent a letter to the Ankara public prosecutor's office, stating that almost all of the defendants in the case had complained of ill-treatment by the security forces. In this connection, he maintained that the complainants had taken part in a demonstration against F-type prisons. Although before intervening and making arrests the police had given the demonstrators a warning and had ordered them to disperse, the demonstrators had resisted the police and thrown stones. In January 2004 the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance acquitted the applicant on account of lack of evidence. The Ministry of the Interior lodged an action for compensation against the applicant and the other co-accused and requested the reimbursement of the amount of compensation paid to the injured police officers. According to the information available in the file, the compensation proceedings were apparently still pending on the date on which the present judgment was adopted. The court's reasoned decision refers to evidence such as eye-witness reports, video recordings of the Security Directorate, video recording of TRT and other national television channels and other material evidence. It refers to the decision of 30 January 2001 to refer the case to the closest assize court.

name: Şükran Yıldız
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4661/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the length of the applicant’s detention on remand, the right to have the lawfulness of her detention decided by a court to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was born in 1980 and lives in Diyarbakır. She was taken into custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the PKK. The Diyarbakır State Security Court concluded that the woman was a member of the PKK and accordingly sentenced her to eight years and four months’ imprisonment. The court refused to release the woman on account of the nature of the alleged offence and the state of evidence. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first-instance court on 20 December 1999. On 9 April 2002 the court rendered its judgment and sentenced the woman to 8 years and 4 months' imprisonment pursuant to Article 168 of the Criminal Code. On 10 August 2001 the court released the woman pending trial. The conviction was upheld on 7 October 2002.

The case originated in an application (no. 4661/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 3 July 2007 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the length of the applicant’s detention on remand to the Government. In the subsequent hearing, the applicant was allowed to have access to a lawyer for the first time. The application was dismissed on 17 July 2007. The applicant was granted a retrial on 21 June 2001. The trial started on 2 December 2006. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal. On 2 June 1999 the Diyarbakır State Security Court concluded that the woman was a member of the PKK and accordingly sentenced her to eight years and four months’ imprisonment. On 10 August 2001 the Court of Cassation quashed the first-instance court's decision. On 9 April 2002 the court rendered its judgment and sentenced the woman to eight-and-a-half years in prison. On 7 October 2002 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court and released the woman pending trial. On 8 August 2003 the Court of Cassation reinstated the judgment and sentenced the woman back to prison.

name: Ilknur Gursoy
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 20597/04) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Mr W.L. Weh, a lawyer practising in Bregenz. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador F. Trauttmansdorff, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 5 September 2006. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the case at the same time. The applicant entered with a valid visa, it had expired, following which her stay in Austria was in breach of the Aliens Act. She alleged, inter alia, that the first-instance decision did not comply with EC law. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Administrative Court and the Constitutional Court. The Administrative Court declined to deal with the applicant’s case, finding that it did not raise important legal issues. On 1 December 2003 that decision was served on the applicant's counsel. It concluded that the applicant had disregarded her visa's validity period. Following which her sojourn was unlawful and she was jailed for 30 hours in default.

name: Hilmi İzmirli
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of a violation of his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. On 12 September 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the convention, it decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The Court decided that the application was not in breach of the European Convention on Human Rights. The application was decided to be heard as part of a larger case against the Turkish Government. Both the defendants and the prosecutor appealed to the Military Court of Cassation. While the appeal was pending, the applicant was released from prison on 14 November 1988. In the meantime, martial law was terminated. Following the promulgation of the Law of 27 December 1993 abolishing the jurisdiction of the martial law courts, the Court ofCassation acquired jurisdiction over the case. The case was transferred to the Ankara Assize Court, which held its first hearing on 6 May 1996. On 16 July 2002 the Assizes Court handed down its verdict on the applicant and numerous other accused. The applicant appealed against this judgment and the proceedings are still pending.

The applicant complained of a violation of his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. He was detained on suspicion of being a member of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. One of the judges dissented, opining that the case should not have been heard at all. The applicant was released from prison on 14 November 1988. While the appeal was pending, martial law was terminated. Following the promulgation of the Law of 27 December 1993 abolishing the jurisdiction of the martial law courts, the Court of Cassation acquired jurisdiction over the case. In October 2006 the Ankara Assize Court convicted the applicant, under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code, of attempting to undermine the constitutional order and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The applicant appealed against this judgment and the proceedings are still pending before the Courtof Cassation. name: Nigar Gözüm
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4789/10) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that there had been a violation of Article 8 of the convention on account of the refusal by the national authorities to indicate her forename in the civil register of births as that of the mother of her adopted child. She argued that in relation to single-parent adoptions there was a lacuna in the Civil Code which required the court to make provision for such a situation. The decision of 22 May 2007, which became final on 20 July of that year, authorised the applicant to adopt a child. In 2008 the court dismissed the applicant’s request on the ground that it had no legal basis. On 14 April 2008 the applicant appealed on points of law. On 15 March 2009 a new regulation entered into force entitled “Regulation on the implementation of mediation services for the adoption of minors’ (“the Regulation”) On 9 November 2010 she applied to the registry office for the registration of her forename as that of the mother of E., relying on Article 20 § 4 of the new Regulation. That request was granted on the same day and the record entries concerning the child were consequently amended with immediate effect. On 5 November 2009 the Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the court below in a judgment which made no mention of the legislative changes.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21272/12) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that she had been compelled to give evidence that would have enabled one or more journalistic sources to be identified, in violation of her right to receive and impart information. The Norwegian Government were represented by Mr C. Reusch of the Attorney General’s Office (Civil Matters) as their Agent. On 23 October 2013 notice of the application was given to the Government. The application was brought by a Norwegian national, Ms C. Langum Becker, on 13 March 2012. The price of DNO stock fell by 4.1% on Monday 27 August 2007. The Oslo stock exchange suspected market manipulation. Mr X confirmed that he had initiated the letter and been the source of the article in DN.no. The applicant refused to answer questions about possible contacts between her and Mr X and other sources, if any, related to the publication by DN. no on August 25, 2007. She argued that she was under no obligation to give evidence on those points. The prosecutor requested that the court impose on the applicant to testify against Mr X in February 2011 before the Oslo City Court (tingrett) The applicant was willing to say that she had received the letter on which the article was based by fax on Friday 24 August 2007, at 5.35 p.m. She also stated that the article had been published onDN.no at 3 a.m., on 25 August 2007 and that she considered the information in the letter as price sensitive. The court ruled that the applicant had a duty to give evidence about her contacts with Mr X in relation to the letter of 24 August 2007 from Attorney Y to the bond trustee company. The City Court held: “The obligation to make a statement is, however, limited to the contact with the defendant as a source and not her communication with possible other unknown sources with whom she has been in contact and who may be protected by the protection of sources” Mr X was convicted at first instance in March 2011 and sentenced to a year in prison. The applicant’s appeal against the order would not be forwarded to the High Court until after the City Court's judgment in the case had been delivered. Mr X was sentenced to one year and six months’ imprisonment, of which nine months were suspended for a probationary period of two years. Mr X appealed to the Borgarting High Court (lagmannsrett) against the City Court’s assessment of the evidence and application of the law in relation to the issue of guilt, its procedure and the sentence (see paragraphs 34-36 below) An appeal by the applicant to the Supreme Court was rejected by three votes to two on 30 September 2011 (Norsk Retstidende – Rt. 2011 page 1266). The appeal had been directed at the High Court's assessment of evidence as well as its application. The majority observed that it did not appear from the wording of Article 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that it was relevant. The law did not give decisive weight. whether the source had disclosed his or her role or that this role had in other ways become known. An obligation on the press to give evidence in such cases was not thought likely to weaken the public’s general trust that the press would protect its sources. A person who so consented could do so, trusting that the recipient of the information would respect the protection of sources as long as the identity of the source was unknown. Once an informant had confirmed that he or she was the source, this fact would become known and the recipient would not want to reveal it. In such a situation, an exemption would in reality not constitute a protection against having to disclose the source. But rather a right to avoid contributing. The majority held that this provision did not apply when the source had come forward and had confirmed his or her role. The principal justification for source protection, as elaborated by the Court in its case-law, was based on the consequences that the disclosure of a source’s identity might have for the free flow of information. The charge in this case had been based. on the fact that the journalist had allowed herself to be used by the source. The majority further noted that there was no decision where the Court had examined the situation where the Source had come. forward and where in this sense there wasNo source to protect (“ingen kilde å beskytte”) The Court of Criminal Procedure allows journalists to refuse to answer questions about their sources. The question was whether a journalist might rely on source protection if the source, without the journalist having revealed it, could be identified with more or less certainty by other evidence. The protection of sources by journalists was, according to the European Court’s case-law, “one of the basic conditions for press freedom” (Goodwin, cited above, § 39). If journalists were allowed to protect their sources, they would obtain information enabling them to uncover matters in society that were worthy of criticism more easily than they would otherwise. If the hearing of evidence on the identity of a source were to be allowed, the media's working conditions would become considerably more constricted and society's interest in free communication of information would suffer. Mr X's appeal against the City Court’s judgment of 3 March 2011 (see paragraph 17 above) was examined by the High Court, which summoned and heard the applicant as a witness on 13 January. It should not be permissible for press journalists to confirm or deny that a person claiming to be the source was in fact the source, even where there was weighty evidence to this effect. Free speech did not protect only information and views that were positively received, but also those which offended, shocked or disturbed the State or parts of the population. Therefore, the fundamental right of journalists to protect their sources could not be dependent on the sources’ motives. The court records contain the following passage: ‘When heard as a witness [the applicant] stated that she had received Attorney [Y]’s letter by fax on 24 August 2007 at 5.35 p.m.’ She answered certain questions but affirmed that she still would not reply to questions about her contacts with Mr X. The presiding judge underlined that an omission to reply to such questions could constitute a ground for the imposition of a fine for an offence against the good order of court proceedings [“rettergangsbot”]. It was emphasised that the duty to reply lay on the witness personally and that a possible fine would be imposed on her personally. There is extensive Supreme Court case-law concerning the main rule in Article 125 § 1 about the protection of journalists’ sources. When an answer is given, the court may decide that it shall only be given to the court and the parties at a sitting in camera and under an order to observe a duty of secrecy. If the author or source has revealed matters that it was socially important to disclose, the witness may be ordered to reveal the name only when this is found to be particularly necessary. The provisions of this section apply correspondingly to any director or employee of any broadcasting agency. “Some authorities refer to a journalistic ‘privilege’ not to disclose a source’s identity, but both reporter and source enjoy rights that may be limited.” National laws should ensure that protections apply strictly, with extremely limited exceptions. Any restrictions must be genuinely exceptional and subject to the highest standards, implemented by judicial authorities only. Such situations should be limited to investigations of the most serious crimes or the protection of the life of other individuals. Revealing or coercing the revelation of the identity of a source creates disincentives for disclosure, dries up further sources to report a story accurately and damages an important tool of accountability. Under Belgian law, journalists and editorial staff may be compelled by a judge to disclose information sources only if they are of a nature that pose a serious threat to the physical integrity of one or more persons. Disclosure of information identifying a source should not be deemed necessary unless it can be convincingly established that: i. reasonable alternative measures to the disclosure do not exist or have been exhausted by the persons or public authorities that seek the disclosure, and ii. the legitimate interest in the disclosure clearly outweighs the public interest. The above requirements should be applied at all stages of any proceedings where the right of non-disclosure might be invoked. In the present case, it is necessary to protect all kinds of information which are likely to lead to the identification of a source. The potential to identify a source determines the type of protected information and the range of such protection.

The High Court, by a decision of 25 January 2012, ordered the applicant to pay a fine of 30,000 Norwegian kroner (NOK), approximately 3,700 euro (EUR) for an offence against the good order of court proceedings. The applicant did not appeal against that decision. By a judgment of the same date, the High Court convicted Mr X and sentenced him to one year and six months’ imprisonment. In 2011 the UN Human Rights Committee adopted General Comment no. 34 concerning Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (CCPR/C/GC/34) which reads: “States parties should recognize and respect that element of the right of freedom of expression that embraces the limited journalistic privilege not to disclose information sources” Under Belgian law, journalists and editorial staff may be compelled by a judge to disclose information sources only if they are of a nature to prevent crimes. The same conditions apply to investigative measures, such as searches, seizures and telephone tapping, with respect to journalistic sources. Other international instruments concerning the protection of journalistic sources include the Resolution on Journalistic Freedoms and Human Rights, adopted at the 4th European Ministerial Conference on Mass Media Policy (Prague, 7-8 December 1994) and Recommendation No. R (2000) 7 on the right of journalists not to disclose their sources of information, adopted by the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe on 8 March 2000. Disclosure of information identifying a source should not be deemed necessary unless it can be convincingly established that: i. reasonable alternative measures to the disclosure do not exist or have been exhausted by the persons or public authorities that seek the disclosure, and ii. the legitimate interest in the disclosure clearly outweighs the public interest. The above requirements should be applied at all stages of any proceedings where the right of non-disclosure might be invoked. name: Fikret Doğan
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court. The application was transferred to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 11 January 2000, the Chamber retained the complaints concerning the right to the fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal and declared the remainder of his complaints inadmissible. The case was heard by the European Court of Justice. In 1982 the Military Public Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Martial Law Court against the applicant and 722 other defendants. The public prosecutor accused the applicant of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the Dev-Yol. He further charged the applicant with having been involved in a number of crimes, such as bomb attacks on several premises, the killing of three persons and an attempt to kill another. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The applicant was sentenced to life imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in public service and placed him under judicial guardianship. In 1995 the Court of Cassation upheld the applicant’s conviction.

By a decision of 11 January 2000, the Chamber retained the complaint and declared the rest of the case inadmissible. The case was settled by a majority decision in favour of the applicant. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. In 1995 the Court of Cassation upheld the applicant’s conviction.

name: Richard Anderson
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 19859/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The applicant was born in 1952 and lives in Glasgow. He is an advocate by profession. He owned a flat in a tenement building in Edinburgh. A number of the flats in the building were also owned by a commercial property company. In 1988, when the proprietors of the building failed to carry out repairs mandated by the city council under statutory notices, the council itself instructed works to be carried out. The applicant claimed that both sets of repairs constituted trespass to his property. The applicant brought proceedings against the commercial property company (“the first defenders”) and the city council (‘the second defenders’) in the Outer House of the Court of Session. He alleged that the statutory notices were invalid on grounds of fraud and illegal conspiracy. By judgments of 17 February 1999, the Sheriff Court rejected the applicant’s claims. The applicant was then informed by the court that he was required to intimate a copy of the closed record to the relevant sheriff clerk. The Lord Ordinary granted the first defenders leave to reclaim (appeal) to the Inner House against the interlocutor of 22 September 1998 in so far as it related to disclosure of documents. The first defenders failed to apply for a hearing. Inner House directed the parties to lodge their grounds of appeal within 28 days. The interlocutory appeal was duly heard on 15 March 2001 and, in a judgment given the same day, the Inner House allowed the first defenders’ reclaiming motion. The Lord Ordinary found the applicant’s claims to be unfounded and unspecified. The appeal was heard on 21 June 2002. As a result of that hearing, the applicant's action was dismissed on 4 September 2002 by the Outer House. On 13 November 2003, the court allowed him to abandon his appeal against the second defenders and proceed only against the first. The applicant was found liable for the first defenders’ costs on 18 December 2003. The appeal was unanimously dismissed on 11 December 2003, the court finding that the applicant’s pleadings lacked specification. Complaints made in relation to the solicitors and advocates representing the council were dismissed by their respective professional bodies and then by the Scottish Legal Services Ombudsman on 13 November 2001 and 4 July 2003, respectively. on 18 and 19 November 2003. In June 2002 the applicant also sought to bring proceedings in the Court of Session against the solicitor acting for the council in the Sheriff Court proceedings. The application for leave to proceed without the signature on the summons was refused on 25 July 2002.

name: Nigel Eastaway
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that there had been a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Court declared the application admissible on 18 November 2003. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The case was returned to the Court of Appeal for reconsideration on 7 February 2010. The applicant and three other defendants were charged in the Blackspur proceedings on 1 July 1992. The Secretary of State’s evidence was completed and served on the applicant on 14 December 1992. On 13 May 1993 the applicant applied to strike out the proceedings. The applicant and one other defendant were acquitted, and two defendants were convicted. On appeal, the two convictions were quashed in February 1995. The Court of Appeal found that the reasons for the Secretary of States’ failure to complete his evidence before the proceedings were commenced had been ‘far from satisfactory’ but considered nonetheless that the case should continue. The appeal to the High Court brought by the first defendant to the disqualification proceeding, Mr Davies, could proceed and was dismissed on 2 May 1995. In November 1995 Mr Davies was granted leave to appeal out of time to the Court of appeal. The defendants were ordered to serve their evidence by 17 January 1997. The Secretary of State gave them until 30 June 1997 to do so. The case was adjourned until 9 February 1998. At that point the defendants were given an extension to serve the evidence. The court ruled that the case should continue as it was in the public interest. The trial was finally settled on 14 June 1998. The judge found in favour of the defendants, and they were allowed to settle the case out of court. The jury found that the defendants had breached the terms of their bail. The decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal and the case was thrown out of the courts. The applicant approached the Secretary of State to negotiate a ‘Carecraft’ settlement. On 30 June 1999 the applicant applied for judicial review of the legality of the secretary of state’s decision not to discontinue the proceedings on grounds of delay. The application was refused by the Court of Appeal on 15 March 2000, following an oral hearing. On 23 March 2000 Buxton LJ refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. In the course of a considered judgment, Lord Justice Buxton described the application as “misconceived’, because the arguments on delay could, and should, have been made in the. course of the disqualification proceedings. The applicant appealed to the House of Lords, which granted leave on 11 July 2000. The House heard the applicant’s appeal on 18 October 2000, and on 2 November 2000 delivered judgment dismissing it. The application was heard by the Vice-Chancellor on 7 February 2001, and judgment was delivered dismissing it on 15 February 2001. In the judgments of the Court of Appeal given in November 1997, Mr Eastaway was granted leave to appeal against the decision of the Secretary of State to continue the proceedings. In this case the application was dismissed on the grounds that the House had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal from the decision. The decision on appeal was made by the Supreme Court on 17 November 2001. A very large proportion of the undoubtedly long time which has elapsed since these proceedings were commenced is due to the various actions taken by Mr Eastaway. Those actions were taken not to obtain but to avoid a fair and public hearing by an independent or impartial tribunal either within a reasonable time or at all. In my view there has been no breach of MrEastaway’s Convention rights under Article 6 and for the Secretary of State now to proceed with these proceedings would not be incompatible with them.” In Re Blackspur Group [1998] 1 WLR 422, 427H and 433B it was recorded that Mr Davies did not suggest then that a fair trial was impossible.

The parties replied to the Court in writing. The case continues. Criminal charges had been brought against the applicant and three other defendants in the Blackspur proceedings on 1 July 1992. The Secretary of State’s evidence was completed and served on the applicant on 14 December 1992. On 13 May 1993 the applicant applied to strike out the proceedings. In November 1995 Mr Davies was granted leave to appeal out of time to the Court of Appeal, and his substantive appeal was dismissed by that court on 24 May 1996. The application was dismissed on 2 May 1995. The appeal to the High Court brought by the first defendant to the disqualification proceeding, Mr Davies, against the Registrar's decision of 27 January 1994, could proceed. The defendants were ordered to serve their evidence by 17 January 1997. They failed to comply and were given an extension by the Secretary of State. On 5 February 1998 the court ruled that the hearing should continue until the defendants had served their evidence. The case was adjourned until 9 March 1998 when it was decided that it was not in the public interest to continue the trial. The judge ruled in favour of the defendants and the case was dismissed. The decision was made to proceed with the case against the defendants in the Supreme Court. The appeal was denied and the court returned to the original hearing date of 17 January 1998. The defendants were allowed to give evidence until 10 July 1997. The hearing was then adjourned again until 9 February 1998, when the judge ruled that there was no need to continue. The applicant went to the Secretary of State to negotiate a ‘Carecraft’ settlement. He was told he would have to accept a disqualification period of five years. On 5 March 1998 the applicant's solicitor sent a draft 'Carecraft' statement. At a directions hearing on 23 March 1998, the time-limit for the applicant’s further evidence was extended indefinitely. On 8 December 1998 the matter was set down for trial on 4 October 1999. On 18 August 1999 the applicant applied for judicial review of the legality of the decision of 30 June 1999, not to discontinue the proceedings on grounds of delay. On 2 February 2000, the applicant renewed his judicial review application before the Court of Appeal. It was refused by the court on 15 March 2000. The Human Rights Act 1998 came into force on 2 October 2000, and on 10 November 2000 the applicant issued an application in the Companies Court to strike out or dismiss the disqualification proceedings. The applicant appealed to the House of Lords, which granted leave on 11 July 2000. The House heard the applicant’s appeal on 18 October 2000 and on 2 November 2000 delivered judgment dismissing it on the grounds that the House had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal from the decision of the Court of Appeal refusing leave to apply for judicial review. The application was heard by the Vice-Chancellor on 7 February 2001, and judgment was delivered dismissal it on 15 February 2001. The applicant took various actions to avoid a fair and public hearing by an independent or impartial tribunal either within a reasonable time or at all. In my view there has been no breach of Mr Eastaway’s Convention rights under Article 6 and for the Secretary of State now to proceed with these proceedings would not be incompatible with them. The applicant signed an undertaking on 31 May 2001 which provided for an agreed period of disqualification of four and a half years, commencing on 25 June 2001. The undertaking was accepted and the proceedings against the applicant were terminated on 4 June 2001, and the case was dismissed on 26 July 2001.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 19 February 1993. It originated in an application (no. 14220/88) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swedish national, Mr Göran Ravnsborg, on 2 July 1988. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings. The President granted him leave to present his own case (Rule 30). The applicant, a university lecturer in law, is a Swedish citizen. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 October 1993. The Court heard addresses by Ms Jagander, Mr Gaukur Jörundsson and Mr Ravnsborg. The applicant, on his own and Mrs Schieck’s behalf, filed a counter-claim and sought the immediate dismissal of the case. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), which ruled in favour of the applicant. The ECHR ruled that the application was not in breach of Article 50 (art. 50) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant was ordered by the relevant courts, under Chapter 9, Article 5, of the Code of Judicial Procedure (rättegångsbalken), to pay fines for improper (otillbörliga) statements made in his written observations. Referring to Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention, he asked for a public hearing. The orders were made in the form of decisions (beslut). He appears to have paid the fines. The first fine was a fine of 1,000 Swedish kronor. The second fine was for $1,000. The applicant appealed against the decision to dismiss him and his wife. The Court of Appeal upheld the decision and ordered the applicant to pay a further fine of 1,000 kronor. The applicant then applied to the Supreme Court for leave to appeal, alleging that the lower and appellate courts had not only denied him a fair trial but had also violated his right to freedom of expression. He expressed the opinion that the likelihood of his being granted leave to appealed was very small in view of the “generally lethargic[,]... lax and allergic attitude of the final instance“, which resulted from the ‘anti-human rights indoctrination received by its members during their many years’ service’ The applicant, on his own behalf and on that of Mrs Schieck’s estate (the latter had died on 7 July 1987), applied to the Supreme Court for leave to appeal, which was refused on 5 January 1988. The case was heard and dismissed again on 9 January 1988 and the appeal was denied. The appeal was decided and dismissed as a result of the appeal being unsuccessful. The judge ruled that the case should be dismissed and sent it back to the Court of Appeal.

The applicant, on his own behalf and on that of Mrs Schieck’s estate, applied to the Supreme Court for leave to appeal, which was refused on 5 January 1988 (in a different decision from that referred to in paragraph 14 above) The Supreme Court. did not hold a hearing. in this case. The decision was overturned by the European Court of Human Rights. in September 1987. In September 1987, the European court of human rights ruled in favour of the applicant in the case of a case relating to the death of a German woman. The hearing was not held. and the decision was upheld by the High Court. in October 1987.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 19 February 1993. It originated in an application (no. 14220/88) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swedish national, Mr Göran Ravnsborg, on 2 July 1988. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 ( art. 6-1) The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs E. Palm, the elected judge of Swedish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 October 1993. The Court heard addresses by Ms Jagander, Mr Gaukur Jörundsson and Mr Ravnsborg. The Commission produced a number of documents, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions, and the applicant submitted his claims under Article 50 (art. 50) The applicant, a university lecturer in law, is a Swedish citizen and lives in Lund in Sweden. The applicant was appointed administrator for his adoptive mother, Mrs Karin Schieck, and her friend, Mrs Marie Åkerblom. He stopped paying the fees for the nursing home when he realised that it was a charitable association. Three times the applicant was ordered by the relevant courts to pay fines for improper (otillbörliga) statements made in his written observations. The orders were made in the form of decisions (beslut). He appears to have paid the fines. The first fine was a fine of 1,000 Swedish kronor. The second fine was for a public hearing. The third fine was an order to pay a fine for a breach of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention (rättegångsbalken; see paragraphs 19-20 below). The fourth fine was in relation to a violation of Article 9, Article 5, of the Code of Judicial Procedure. The applicant argued that the likelihood of his being granted leave to appeal was very small in view of the “generally lethargic[,]... lax and allergic attitude of the final instance’. He alleged that one of its members, whom he named, had a “far-reaching tendentiously fascist way of presiding’ over the court and was “grossly partial in favour of municipal interests, collegiate corruption and abuse of public power through high-handedness, terror and reactionary principles“ The Court of Appeal confirmed the District Court’s decision and ordered the applicant to pay a further fine of 1,000 kronor. On 4 November 1987, in a separate decision from the one mentioned in paragraph 13 above, the Court of appeal rejected the appeal. The applicant, on his own behalf and on that of Mrs Schieck’s estate, applied to the Supreme Court for leave to appeal, which was refused on 5 January 1988 (in a different decision from that referred to in paragraph 14 above) The Supreme Court did not hold a hearing. The applicant appealed to the European Court of Human Rights. The European Court refused to hear the appeal, and the appeal was dismissed. The appeal was heard in March 1989, but the case was thrown out on appeal. The application was eventually dismissed on appeal in March 1990. The case was heard again in May 1990, but was dismissed again on appeal on August 1991.

name: Mehmet Erdagöz
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the Government of the Republic of Turkey (“the Government”) on 18 September 1996. It originated in an application (no. 21890/93) against Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under Article 25. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr F. Gölcüklü, the elected judge of Turkish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention), and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 26 June 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mr Martínez, Mr Kaplan, Mr Yılmaz and Mrs Akçay. Mr Walsh was unable to take part in the deliberations on 22 September 1997, Sir John Freeland, substitute judge, replaced him as a member of the Chamber. The outcome of these proceedings is not known. The circumstances of the case are as follows: A brawl broke out between the applicant and members of his family on one side and a Mr H.A. and his friends on the other. The police arrived on the scene half an hour later – before the applicant, who was not on the premises, had even been informed – noted that the windows had been broken. H.A. was charged with threatening use of a firearm, criminal damage and an offence under the Firearms Act. In a judgment of 28 June 1993 the Criminal Court acquitted him for lack of sufficient evidence. Court of Cassation upheld this judgment on 28 February 1994. Deprivation of the applicant’s liberty was found to be a breach of his right to freedom of movement. He was ordered to be transferred, together with H.A., who had been arrested in the meantime, to the security police headquarters. Mr Erdagöz has frequently lodged ill-founded complaints against the station personnel, that there is animosity between him and [H. a.], that he has previously abused the police and the judicial authorities. The applicant alleged that during the inquiries into the altercation of 3 June 1992 the former had abused his authority by drawing up a biased report of the incident. He accused S.K. of inflicting ill-treatment on him when he first went to the police station, at 5.30 a.m., following the events of the night of 15 to 16 September. The next day, at the request of the police, Mr Erdagöz had a medical examination at the social security hospital in Adana. The provisional report, drawn up on the same day, mentions the following injuries: superficial grazing on the left side of the back and bruises and swelling below both knees. On 24 December 1992 a doctor from the Adana Institute of Forensic Medicine drew up a new report confirming the findings. Mehmet Erdagöz was charged with falsely reporting a criminal offence. He was also accused of insulting a policeman who took him into police custody for forty-eight hours. The case was dismissed on appeal on 23 February 1993 and he appealed to the Minister of Justice. The appeal was refused on 29 March 1993 and the case was dropped on 6 December 1993. He appealed again on 27 January 1993 to the President of the Tarsus Assize Court, who dismissed the appeal in March 1993. The second complaint he made against the policeman was dismissed in April 1993 on appeal. The third complaint against the officer, A.K., was dropped in June 1993. The applicant was suspected of falsely reporting a criminal offence. He was held for twenty-four hours so that the inquiry could be completed. On 15 February 1994 the applicant appealed against the above discontinuation order. On 7 March 1994 the President of the Tarsus Assize Court dismissed the appeal. On 24 June 1994 the Minister of Justice refused a petition in which Mr Erdagöz had asked him to lodge an appeal in the interests of the law.‘There is no evidence to support the allegations of defamation.’ The appeal was dismissed in March 1994 and the case was dismissed on 23 June 1994. ‘The applicant’s detention in police custody had lasted for two days and had been due to the resentment the police felt towards him’

The applicant was transferred, together with H.A., who had been arrested in the meantime, to the security police headquarters. He was suspected of fabricating evidence and of abusing the police and the judicial authorities. The application was dismissed on 8 February 1994, and he was released on bail. The case was heard at the High Court of Justice. The applicant alleges the chief inspector drew up a biased report of the altercation of 3 June 1992. Mr Erdagöz also accused Deputy Inspector S.K. of inflicting ill-treatment on him when he first went to the police station, at 5.30 a.m., following the events of the night of 15 to 16 September. The Adana public prosecutor, after conducting an investigation, concluded that the allegation of abusing authority was unfounded and decided not to pursue the investigation. The applicant was released the same day, at a time which has not been specified. The complaint was dropped after the public prosecutor concluded that it was unfounded. The first complaint was made on 17 September 1992 and the second on 18 September 1992. The complainant was taken into police custody even though he was the complainant. Mehmet Erdagöz was charged with falsely reporting a criminal offence. But the case was dropped after the applicant appealed against the discontinuation of the proceedings against the two police officers. As the police had not found any pertinent evidence that the offence had been committed, the complainant was referred to the public prosecutor’s office by an order of 17 September 1992. He alleged in particular that his detention in police custody had lasted for two days and had been due to the resentment the police felt towards him. The President of the Tarsus Assize Court dismissed the appeal and on 24 June 1994 the Minister of Justice refused a petition in which Mr Erdagöz had asked him to lodge an appeal in the interests of the law.

name: Mehmet Ali Ege
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Mehmet Ali Ege (“the applicant”), was represented by Mr Ö. Öneren, a lawyer practising in Ankara. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the criminal proceedings. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was tried before the Diyarbakır Martial Law Court. The Military Court of Cassation quashed the judgment on the ground that the latter had misinterpreted the domestic law in respect of the offence in question. The applicant was released from detention on 29 July 1990. On 13 July 1998 the criminal proceedings against the applicant were terminated on the grounds that the statutory time limit under Articles 102 and 104 of the Criminal Code had expired. The case was closed on the basis that the applicant had not been found guilty of any offence under the Turkish Penal. Code. The application was dismissed by the court on 2 August 1998.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 74039/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Van Civil Court awarded the applicant TRL 47,273,000 plus interest calculated at three different rates depending on the relevant period of time. The applicant appealed. name: Özgür Keskin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 12305/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1974 and lives in İzmir. On 19 March 2007 he resigned from his job to perform his military service. The court held that the applicant’s discharge from the military shortly after he had been enlisted fell under the provision of the collective agreement, which called for the suspension of the employment contract when an employee was conscripted for reasons other than compulsory military service, such as being recalled to the armed forces in times of war. The City Council appealed against the decision and reserved its right to submit additional observations once the reasoned judgment of the first-instance court had been served on it. That appeal was not communicated to the applicant. On 21 July 2008, following an examination based on the case file, the Court of Cassation quashed the first‑instance court’s judgment and found in favour of the City Council. It found it established that the applicant had resigned from his job to perform his military service and that he had been paid severance pay. It held that a rejection of the applicant's request for reinstatement could not be regarded as the termination of his employment contract. No appeal was possible against this decision.

name: Martin Zumtobel
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 1 September 1992. It originated in an application (no. 12235/86) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by the firm of F.M. Zumtobel. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 ( art. 6-1) The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them. The case concerns expropriation proceedings instituted with a view to the construction in the province of Vorarlberg of a provincial highway. It appears that the scheme in question dated back to 1960, but that opposition from local landowners had prevented its realisation. The authorities conducted an investigation into inter alia whether the projected road was compatible with the requirements of environmental protection (Landschaftsschutz). The proposed route was published (zur öffentlichen Einsichtnahme aufgelegt) and the file made available for consultation at the Rankweil council offices from 1 to 31 October 1984. The first applicant repeatedly but unsuccessfully requested to be allowed to study various documents in the file. The authorities consulted several experts. According to the highways expert and the road traffic expert, the proposed section of highway was important because it would improve traffic links between Rankweil and Feldkirch. The Zumtobel partnership thereupon applied to the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) It claimed that the expropriation proceedings, which were subject to final review, had violated its right of access to a court with full jurisdiction. The Office considered the first request to be irrelevant to the case; as to the second it stated that the official expert had not shown any bias in favour of the authorities. The first applicant also challenged the decision of 13 February 1986 (see paragraph 10 above) in the Administrative Court. Relying on substantially the same arguments as in the Constitutional Court, it now complained of breaches of procedural and substantive law. The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 22 September 1989, after a purely written procedure; the applicants had not asked it to hold a hearing. In the court’s opinion, the complaint that the scheme objected to was not based on any reasonable overall plan was not enough to establish that the contested decision had been unlawful. The court held that the applicant partnership had also failed to cast doubt on the official experts’ reports. The court considered that mere general remarks on the independence of official experts were not enough to prove a specific legitimate doubt for the purposes of the 1950 Law. The fact that such an expert took part in proceedings to which the Province was a party did not, unless there were special circumstances, constitute a serious reason to doubt his complete impartiality. As the applicant partnership had not been a party to the environmental protection proceedings (Landschaftsschutzverfahren), it could not claim a right to be heard in the case. The court also rejected the complaints relating to the hearing of the official experts. with reference to the complaints of lack of access to the case file. There was nothing to show that these documents could have been material to the applicant partnership’s case or that the Office had based its decision on them. The Administrative Court also found that there had been no breach of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention and declined to refer the matter to the Constitutional Court. The first applicant had meanwhile applied to the Feldkirch District Court (Bezirksgericht) to determine the amount of compensation. On 17 December 1987 this was set at 9,963,032.50 Austrian schillings (ATS). On 28 May 1988, on appeal (Rekurs), the amount was reduced to ATS 4,560,000. The first applicant’s appeal on points of law (Revisionsrekurs) against this decision was dismissed by the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) October 1988 the first applicant's appeal on Points of Law was dismissed. October 1988  the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. The appeal was dismissed on the basis that the decision was not in line with the law of the country at the time. The Supreme Court said that the appeal was not on the grounds of a breach of the law, but rather of the principle of the right to appeal the decision of the High Court of Justice. The decision was upheld on appeal on October 1988.

The first applicant had meanwhile applied to the Feldkirch District Court (Bezirksgericht) to determine the amount of compensation. On 17 December 1987 this was set at 9,963,032.50 Austrian schillings (ATS) On 28 May 1988, on appeal (Rekurs) the amount was reduced to ATS 4,560,000.50 (ATS). On 6 December 1987, the first applicant applied for compensation. The applicant had twice been sentenced to terms of imprisonment of at least one year (for several acts of fraud, embezzlement, theft and burglary). Since the age of 20, he has committed different types of increasingly serious offences against the property of others. He did not feel like working and financed his very costly lifestyle through crime. He had a disposition to commit serious offences and was therefore dangerous to the public. On 2 March 1994, he served the remainder of the sentence imposed on him in the judgment of 1972. Until 19 April 1994 he then served a further prison sentence imposed by the Cologne Regional Court. Since 26 January 2000 the applicant, having served the sentence imposed in the judgment of 1997, has been in preventive detention. Despite the fact that he had repeatedly served long prison sentences, the applicant had kept committing increasingly serious offences for fifty years in order to obtain substantial amounts of money. As confirmed by the convincing report of a psychiatric and neurological expert, Sa., it was to be expected that the applicant would commit further offences against the property of others if released. The proceedings at issue were decided by the Aachen Regional Court and the Cologne Court of Appeal on 11 June 2002, 13 July 2004 and 10 October 2006 respectively. The applicant is still liable to commit offences causing considerable economic damage, as required by Article 66 § 1 of the Criminal Code. The Aachen Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s request for the suspension on probation of his preventive detention as ordered by the Cologne Regional Court on 6 June 1972. The Regional Court found that there was no basis to expect that the applicant, if released, would not commit further serious offences. It declared that no request for review of this decision would be admissible within a one-year period (Article 67e § 3 of the Criminal Code – see paragraph 49 below). The Court also found that it was clear from the report dated 4 January 2007 submitted by the governor of Aac hen Prison that there had not been any developments on the applicant's part warranting a different conclusion. The Cologne Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against the Regional Court’s decision of 14 June 2007. The court referred to a report dated 21 February 2006 by a medical expert, Sch., whom it had previously consulted. The latter had found that the applicant suffered from a personality disorder. This finding, which was still valid, was at the root of his previous offences and was the reason why he risked committing further offences if released. As he had no family or friends outside prison, he could, if anything, be placed in a supervised residence (betreute Wohneinrichtung), but it could not be ascertained whether he was sufficiently ready to cooperate. The Court of Appeal noted that the negative prognosis as to the applicant’s future conduct could partly have been caused by misconduct on the part of the Aachen Prison management. The public interest in the detention of the applicant, who still risked committing serious property offences, continued to prevail over his own interest in personal liberty. name: Aziz Aydın Arslan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28353/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 19 March 2007. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applicant's application at the same time. The applicant was born in 1957 and lives in Istanbul. He was recruited by Türkiye Emlak Bankası A.Ş., a state-owned bank (hereinafter ‘the Bank’). In 1991 he was appointed to the post of deputy director in charge of credit cards. Criminal proceedings were brought against the director of the Topkapı branch of the Bank and three other persons for having committed a fraud. The applicant and the Bank intervened in these proceedings as a third party. On 9 July 1999 the Bakırköy Assize Court in Istanbul convicted the director and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment for having abused his duty. On 29 May 2001 the Court of Cassation quashed the above judgment. On 31 December 2004 the Bak Turkey Assize. Court terminated the criminal proceedings against the. director since they were time-barred. The. applicant appealed against this judgment arguing that the punishment imposed on the director was lenient.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were charged with involvement in a money laundering scheme together with a third co-accused. Two British nationals pleaded guilty to conspiracy to launder the proceeds of criminal conduct contrary to section 1 of the Criminal Law Act 1977. The second applicant was sentenced to four and a half years’ imprisonment and the first applicant to six years' imprisonment. The application was allowed to stand and a decision on the merits of the case was made on 14 June 2007. The case was heard by the Acting President of the Chamber of the Fourth Section. The case was listed for the confiscation hearing with a time-estimate of five working days. Adjournment pending R. v. Steele and Shevki was set for 30 October 2000, outside the six-month period required under section 72A of the CJA 1988. The applicants objected that the court lacked jurisdiction to hear the proceedings. The confiscation proceedings were adjourned to await the outcome of a similar case which was due to be heard by the Court of Appeal, R v Steele and Hervki. On 21 November 2000 Mr E. was granted leave to appeal against his conviction. On 24 November 2000 both the applicants’ applications for appeal against sentence were refused. The Court of Appeal heard and dismissed Mr E.’s appeal against conviction. The substantive hearing of the confiscation hearing was again adjourned. The Crown Court imposed a confiscation order on the second applicant in the amount of GBP 75,350, to be paid within 18 months of the resolution of any appeal to the Court of appeal. The first applicant lodged an application for leave to appeal on the same grounds as the second. The proceedings before the Courtof Appeal were adjourned to 28 January 2002 with a time estimate of three weeks. The confiscation proceedings were again listed for mention on 20 September 2001. The hearing was fixed to begin on 15 October 2001. Second applicant obtained a Certificate of Inadequacy from the High Court. This entitled him to return to the Crown Court to seek a reduction of the confiscation order. The Court of Appeal considered that a high degree of judicial scrutiny was required before finding exceptional circumstances to justify the imposition of a confiscation Order outside the six-month time-limit. They noted that on 29 June 2000, defence counsel for the second applicant and the co-accused Mr. E. had requested an early hearing. However, the earliest date that the trial judge would be available was the week beginning 30 October 2000. That date was pencilled in, even though it was “more than four months away” The House of Lords observed that the core problem before it was whether, as a matter of statutory construction, failure to comply with a statutory time-limit would have the effect of invalidating an act. The fact that Parliament cast statutory requirements in imperative form without expressly specifying the consequences had caused a great deal of litigation. In London and Clydeside Estates Ltd v. Aberdeen District Council [1980] 1 WLR 182, 189E-190C, Lord Hailsham had emphasised that it was within the courts’ inherently discretionary jurisdiction to determine the nature of a particular statutory requirement. The Law Lords rejected the applicants’ argument. The prime purpose behind the statutory provision for confiscation orders was the recovery of any financial benefit that an offender might have obtained from his criminal conduct. Court of Appeal re-imposed the confiscation orders and sentences of imprisonment in default on the applicants in October 2005. That, given the criminal law context, a strict approach to the construction of section 72A of the CJA 1988 should be adopted and instead applied a teleological approach. The prejudice to the applicants was not significant and was outweighed by the countervailing public interest in not allowing convicted offenders to escape confiscation for what were no more than bona fide errors in the judicial process. In any event, there would always be the safeguard of judicial review should there be an apparent abuse of process. The Court of Appeal ruled that the Crown Court had postponed its final decision on confiscation order in good faith.

Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two British nationals, Mr David Frederick Bullen and Mr Kamlesh Kumar Soneji (“the applicants”), were charged with involvement in a money laundering scheme. The applicants were represented by Mr N. Seeley, a lawyer practising in Hertford. The United Kingdom Government (‘the Government’) was represented by their Agent, Ms A. Sharif. The application was given notice to the Government on 14 June 2007. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 §3) The confiscation hearing was set for 30 October 2000, outside the six-month period required under section 72A of the CJA 1988. The applicants objected that the court lacked jurisdiction to hear the confiscation proceedings on the grounds that more than six months had elapsed since their convictions. It was agreed by the parties that the proceedings should be adjourned to await the outcome of a similar case which was due to be heard by the Court of Appeal, R v Steele and Shevki. On 14 December 2000 the Court. of Appeal delivered its judgment in R v. Steele and shevki ([2000] EWCA Crim 70). It found that although adjournments beyond the six.month period prescribed by statute should be avoided, exceptional circumstances such as the unavailability of a judge would not deprive a subsequent confiscation order of its validity. On 26 and 27 March 2001 the Court of Appeal heard and dismissed Mr E.’s appeal against conviction. The substantive hearing of the confiscation hearing was again adjourned. On 7 February 2002 the Crown Court imposed a confiscation order on the first applicant in the sum of GBP 375,000, with a consecutive term of 21 months’ imprisonment to be served in default. The second applicant lodged an application for leave to appeal on the ground that the. Crown Court had no jurisdiction to make it because of the lapse of the six-month period provided by section 72A(3) of the CJA 1988. In 2002 the second applicant obtained a Certificate of Inadequacy from the High Court. This entitled him to return to the Crown Court to seek a reduction of the confiscation order. The Court of Appeal considered that, given the importance attached by Parliament and the courts to the link between confiscation orders and sentencing, a high degree of judicial scrutiny was required before finding exceptional circumstances to justify the imposition of a confiscations order outside the six-month time-limit. The failure to address the question as to whether the circumstances could properly be described as exceptional and to make a finding to that effect was fatal to the upholding of the confiscated orders. The House of Lords reversed the decisions of the Court of Appeal and ordered the latter to re-impose the confiscation orders in respect of both applicants. The key question was whether, as a matter of statutory construction, failure to comply with a statutory time-limit would have the effect of invalidating an act. A distinction had first evolved between mandatory and directory requirements; where a requirement was mandatory, a failure to. comply had the effect on invalidating the act in question but where a. requirement was merely directory, a Failure to comply did not invalidate the act. The Law Lords considered that the prime purpose behind the statutory provision for confiscation. orders was the recovery of any financial benefit that an offender might have. obtained from his criminal conduct. The Court of Appeal re-imposed the confiscation orders and sentences of imprisonment in default on the applicants. The prejudice to the applicants was not significant and was outweighed by the countervailing public interest in not allowing convicted offenders to escape confiscation for what were no more than bona fide errors in the judicial process. In any event, there would always be the safeguard of judicial review should there be an apparent abuse of process. The Supreme Court ruled. that, given the criminal law context, a strict approach to the construction of section 72A of the CJA 1988 should be adopted and. instead applied a teleological approach..
