train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 62543/00) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented by lawyers practising in Pamplona and Madrid. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27) was established. The case was settled on 12 September 2000, with the decision to continue with the construction of the Itoiz dam to be made in the following year. The case originated in an engineering project of February 1989 for the construction of a dam in Itoiz (Navarre province) which would result in the flooding of three nature reserves and a number of small villages. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits. On 1 April 2003 the Chamber decided, having regard to the circumstances of the case, to dismiss a Rule 39 request submitted by the applicants. The case was settled by the Audiencia Nacional in August 2003. The Court of Appeal ruled that the application was admissible and reserved its position on the Government's preliminary questions as to whether the first five applicants lacked ‘victim’ status and had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. The Audiencia Nacional partly upheld the appeal, considering in particular that, according to the law, the planned dam should have been based on the national hydrological plan. The court also accepted the request for precise designation of the protection zones around the nature reserves affected by the dam. In June 1996 the parliament of the Autonomous Community of Navarre (parlamento foral de Navarra) passed Aut autonomous Community Law (foral) no. 9/1996 on natural sites in Navarre. This law amended Autonomous community Law no. 6/1987 of 10 April 1987, particularly with regard to the possibility of reclassifying the protection zone or carrying out. The Audiencia Nacional declared final the interim enforcement measures ordered on 6 March 1996 concerning the prohibition on filling the reservoir and other related work. In a judgment of 14 July 1997, the Supreme Court definitively cancelled the dam project in so far as it concerned the 500-metre protection zones around nature reserves RN 9, 10 and 11. As a result of the judgment, the size of the planned dam, and thus of the area to be flooded, was reduced, so that the village of Itoiz, where the applicants' immovable property was located, was saved from flooding. The Supreme Court later ruled that it had become legally impossible to enforce the judgment. The applicant association contested the authorities' argument, claiming that the Autonomous Community law of 1996 was inapplicable in the instant case. By a decision of 21 May 1998, the Constitutional Court declared the application inadmissible on account of certain errors in its presentation. In order to rectify the above-mentioned errors, the Audiencia Nacional summoned the parties on 28 May 1998 so that it could hear their submissions on certain aspects of the law whose constitutionality had been challenged. The Constitutional Court then declared the issues raised in the preliminary question admissible. The government and parliament of Navarre submitted their observations. The Attorney General's observations were submitted on 29 September 1998. The Audiencia Nacional forwarded to the Constitutional Court the written pleadings submitted by the applicant association during the proceedings before it. The Speaker of the Senate asked that the Senate be considered a party to the proceedings and offered its assistance. The Constitutional Court, sitting as a full court, held that the impugned provisions of the Autonomous Community law of 1996 were compatible with the Constitution. It observed at the outset that enforcement of the Supreme Court's judgment of 14 July 1997 had become impossible since the entry into force of the new law. The Court held that this was not to be seen as a legislative solution for the particular problem of the three peripheral zones around the three nature reserves affected by construction of the Itoiz dam.  Constitutional Court considered that the fact that a new law had been passed amending the legal system applicable to the peripheral protection zones was not in itself incompatible with the right to execution of judicial decisions. It found that both the Supreme Court's judgment of 14 July 1997 and the new Autonomous Community law of 1996 were intended to guarantee the existence of a peripheral protection zone around the three nature reserves affected by the dam's construction. The balance of general interests had been respected and that there was no clear lack of proportion between the conflicting interests. Consequently, the impugned provisions could not be held to be contrary to Article 24 § 1 of the Constitution. The Constitutional Court dismissed the application for a preliminary ruling. The judgment was published in the Official Gazette on 14 April 2000. It was. out that laws could be challenged before the Constitutional Court through the remedy provided for in Article 163 of the Constitution. The application was dismissed by the court and the decision was not published. The appeal was dismissed on 6 December 2000 and the case was settled on 11 December 2000. The case was heard by the South African High Court, which ruled in favour of the applicant. The judge's decision was published on 7 September 2000. It observed at the outset that enforcement of the Supreme Court's judgment of 14 July 1997 had become impossible since the entry into force of the new law. The Speaker of the Senate asked that the Senate be considered a party to the proceedings and offered its assistance. The Constitutional Court ruled that, given the significance of the question raised by the Itoiz dam's construction, which could not simply be ignored, it was justifiable that the explanatory memorandum accompanying the law specifically mentioned the aim and means of environmental protection in the peripheral protection zones around the three nature reserves. The Constitutional Court considered that the fact that a new law had been passed amending the legal system applicable to the peripheral protection zones was not in itself incompatible with the right to execution of judicial decisions. It found that both the Supreme Court's judgment of 14 July 1997 and the new Autonomous Community law of 1996 were intended to guarantee the existence of a peripheral protection zone around the three nature reserves affected by the dam's construction. The balance of general interests had been respected and there was no clear lack of proportion between the conflicting interests. The impugned provisions could not be held to be contrary to Article 24 § 1 of the Constitution. It added that the new law did not amount to ad causam legislation. The Constitutional Court dismissed the application for a preliminary ruling. name: Havva Kaba
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1236/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. According to the applicants, Mr Kaba's exposure to asbestos at Hasköy Dock had caused his cancer. They were also concerned about the allegedly inadequate treatment he received at the GATA military hospital. The applicants were represented by Mr A. Tizik, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government’s” Agent) was represented by their Agent. On 15 September 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time (Article 29 § 1). In January 2004 the applicants again requested legal aid to pay the court fees. The Military Supreme Administrative Court refused to grant the applicants legal aid, once again without giving reasons. The court also decided to discontinue the compensation proceedings because the applicants had not paid the necessary court fees on 4 June 2004. This decision was served on the applicants on 4June 2004. The applicants' lawyer referred to the relevant statements of means provided by the domestic authorities. He stated that while lodging the case he had submitted the relevant medical records concerning Mr Yusuf Kaba, a report on the asbestos levels at Hasköy Dock and an expert report, and that this evidence should be sufficient to prove that they had a well-founded case.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 9 September 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 11 October 1993 by Denmark. The object of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). On 23 February 1994 the President of the Chamber granted leave to Human Rights Watch, a New York based non-governmental human rights organisation, to submit observations on specific aspects of the case (Rule 37 para. 2). The latter’s comments were filed on 23 March. On 23 February the Chamber had authorised (Rule 41 para. 1) the applicant to show the video-recording of the television programme in issue in his case to the judges taking part in the proceedings. A showing was held shortly before the hearing on 20 April. On various dates between 22 March and 15 April 1994 the Commission produced a number of documents and two video-cassettes. The applicant submitted further details on his claims under Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 April 1994. The Court heard addresses by Mr Rozakis, Mr Lehmann, Mr Elmer, Mr Boyle and Mr T. Trier. During the interview, which was conducted by the applicant, the three Greenjackets were asked to answer a question put by the President. The application was brought by Mr Jens Olaf Jersild, a Danish national, who is employed by Danmarks Radio (Danish Broadcasting Corporation), assigned to its Sunday News Magazine (Søndagsavisen) The magazine deals with a range of social and political issues, including xenophobia, immigration and refugees. Interview lasted between five and six hours, of which between two and two and a half hours were video-recorded. Danmarks Radio paid the interviewees fees in accordance with its usual practice. The applicant subsequently edited and cut the film of the interview down to a few minutes. The transcript of the Greenjackets item reads as follows: ‘It’s good being a racist. We believe Denmark is for the Danes.’ ‘The flag on the wall is the flag of the Southern States from the American Civil War, but today it is also the symbol of racism, the Ku Klux Klan, and it shows what Lille Steen, Henrik and Nisse are’ There are 20-25 young people from STUDSEN in the same group. They meet not far away from the public housing area near some old houses which are to be torn down. They reaffirm among other things their racism, their hatred of immigrants and their support for the Ku Klux Klan. A nigger is not a human being, it’s an ape. There is always someone who wants to show off, as if they are better than the white man, but in the long run, it's thewhite man who is better. A lot of people are saying something different. There are many blacks, for example in the USA, who have important jobs. Henrik is one of the strongest supporters of the Klan. He hates the foreign workers, ‘Perkere’ [a very derogatory word in Danish for immigrant workers] They come up here, man, and sponge on our society. But we, we have enough problems in getting our social benefits, man. They just get it. They are the first on the housing list, they get better flats than us. Half of the prison population in ‘Vestre�’ are in there because of drugs, half of those in Vestre prison anyway, they are the people who are serving animal, that goes for all the other foreign workers as well. Per Axholt, known as ‘Pax’ [(P)], is employed in the youth centre in Studsgårdsgade. He has worked there for several years, but many give up a lot sooner because of the tough environment. He feels that the reasons why the young people are persecuting the immigrants is that they are themselves powerless and disappointed. If they could speak, they would say what they want, he says. Just what you and I want. Some control over their lives, work which may be considered decent and which they like. A reasonably functioning family, a wife or a husband and some children, a reasonable middle-class life. Germain 'Perkere' is an 18-year-old who has been involved in crime since the age of 14. He says he has committed his first crime when he was 14 and has had a criminal career since then. Perkere has been pinching videos, where the ‘perkere’ have been our customers, so they have money, he says. He adds: ‘If people want to be out here and have a nice time and be racists and drink beer, and have fun, then it’s quite obvious you don’t want to sit in the slammer.’ Three youths interviewed by the applicant were charged with a violation of Article 266 (b) of the Penal Code (straffeloven) for having made the statements cited below. The Bishop of Ålborg complained to the Minister of Justice. No complaints were made to the Radio Council, which had competence in such matters, or to Danmarks Radio but the Public Prosecutor instituted criminal proceedings in the City Court of Copenhagen (Københavns Byret) against the three youths. “Just take a picture of a gorilla, man, and then look at a nigger, it’s a nigger.” “... the Northern States wanted that the niggers should be free human beings, man. They are not human being, they are animals’ “A nigger is not a human being, it’s an animal, that goes for all the other foreign workers as well, Turks, Yugoslavs and whatever they are called.“ “Half of the prison population in ‘Vestre’ are in there because of drugs ... they are the people who are serving time for dealing drugs ...” “What we don’t like is when they walk around in those Zimbabwe-clothes and then speak this hula-hula language in the street ...’“ The applicant was charged, under Article 266 (b) in conjunction with Article 23, with aiding and abetting the three youths; the same charge was brought against the head of the news section of Danmarks Radio. Three Greenjackets were convicted for making racist statements during a TV interview. The applicant was convicted of aiding and abetting them, as was Mr Jensen, in his capacity as programme controller. They were sentenced to pay day-fines (dagsbøder) totalling 1,000 and 2,000 Danish kroner, respectively, or alternatively to five days’ imprisonment (hæfte). The applicant and Mr Jensen appealed against the City Court’s judgment to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret). They essentially reiterated the submissions made before the City. Court and, in addition, the applicant explained that he had refrained from omitting these from the programme, considering it. The High Court dismissed the appeal by five votes to one in 1988. The Supreme Court (Højesteret) rejected the appeal in a judgment of 13 February 1989. The majority held: “The defendants have caused the publication of the racist statements made by a narrow circle of persons and thereby made those persons liable to punishment” The dissenting member was of the view that, although the statements by the Greenjackets constituted offences under Article 266 (b) of the Penal Code, the applicant and Mr Jensen had not transgressed the bounds of the freedom of speech to be enjoyed by television and other media. He assumed that they were aware that they might incur criminal liability by making the statements and had therefore not warned them. The majority had attached importance to the fact that they had caused the racist statements to be made public. The statements would hardly have been punishable under Article 266 (b) of the Penal Code had they not been made to a wide circle (“videre kreds“) of people. Their news or information value was not such as to justify their dissemination and therefore did not warrant acquitting the defendants. This did not mean that extremist views could not be reported in the press, but such reports must be carried out in a more balanced and comprehensive manner than was the case in the television programme in question. I therefore vote in favour of the defendants’ acquittal. The minority, on the other hand, considered that the right to information overrode the interests protected by Article 266 (b) of the Penal Code. The Greenjackets were a group of young people, calling themselves “the GreenJackets” (“grønjakkerne’), at Østerbro in Copenhagen. name: Claude Mazurek
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34406/97) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 13 December 1996. The application was examined by the Court following the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention on 1 November 1998. On 4 May 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible and decided to invite the parties to submit their observations on the merits at a hearing. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mrs M. Dubrocard, Deputy Director, Human Rights Division, Legal Affairs Department, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, and for the applicant Mr A. Ottan, of the Montpellier Bar. Claude Mazurek is a French national who was born in Avignon in 1942. His mother died on 1 August 1990 of HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) encephalopathy. She left two children: a son, Alain, born out of wedlock in 1936 and legitimised by his mother’s marriage in 1937. Alain brought an action against the applicant in the Nîmes tribunal de grande instance seeking an order that his mother's estate be divided by a notary. In a judgment of 21 January 1993 the court ordered the estate to be divided. With regard to the applicant's rights, it referred to Article 760 of the Civil Code. The Court of Appeal said the amount was not a gift to the child, but part of a legal agreement. The court said the law does not discriminate against children born to a marriage with an illegitimate child. It said the children's interests should be protected by the law, not the child's. The decision was made to split the money between the children and their mother, not to give it to the children as a gift, as had been originally intended. The Court of appeal said this would not be allowed to happen, and that the children would have to pay the full amount back to the parents. The case was returned to the courts, and the decision was upheld. The court was properly entitled to hold that it was not the intention of the legislature to discriminate between children on the grounds of their birth. The applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation, which delivered its judgment on 25 June 1996. In respect of the complaint that the. Court of Appeal had ordered the sum transferred to the applicant’s account to be returned to the. estate to be divided, the Court held that in. deciding that the facts of the case had not shown any intention on the part of the deceased to. bestow a gift on her son in advance of the division of her estate. The Court of. Cassation held that inheritance rights had nothing to do with respect for private and family life guaranteed by Article 8 of the Convention.

The Government submitted their observations on 9 March 1998, after an extension of the time allowed, and the applicant replied on 22 April 1998. The application was examined by the Court following the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention on 1 November 1998. On 4 May 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible and decided to invite the parties to submit their observations. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 12 October 1999. Claude Mazurek was born in 1942 and lives at La Grande-Motte. His mother died on 1 August 1990 of HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) encephalopathy. She left two children: a son, Alain, born out of wedlock in 1936 and legitimised by his mother’s marriage in 1937. On 30 April 1991 Alain brought an action against the applicant in the Nîmes tribunal de grande instance seeking an order that his mother's estate be divided by a notary. In a judgment of 21 January 1993 the court ordered the estate to be divided. With regard to the applicant's rights, it referred to Article 760 of the Civil Code. The Court of Appeal ruled that Article 760 was necessary to protect the interests of all children. The court ruled that the amount was not a gift to the child but was to be shared by all the children of the same family. The decision was made in accordance with Article 8 and Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), which protects the rights of children born to parents who are not in a relationship with the child’s biological parents. The case was heard before the European Court of Justice (ECJ), which has the power to order the division of assets. The ECJ made the decision to order that the money be returned to the father of the child, not the mother. The applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation, which delivered its judgment on 25 June 1996. The court was properly entitled to hold that it was not the intention of the legislature to discriminate between children on the grounds of their birth, but to ensure minimum compliance with the marital obligations of a married parent with regard to his or her legitimate children. The applicant subsequently received one quarter of the sum awarded by the Compensation Fund for Transfusion Patients and Haemophiliacs in 1994. The Court ofCassation held that inheritance rights had nothing to do with respect for private and family life guaranteed by Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

name: Nurcan Güngil
train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by a Turkish national, Ms Nurcan Güngil (“the applicant”), on 30 July 2003. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the civil proceedings. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was represented by Mrs İ. İlimoğlu, a lawyer practising in Ankara. The Turkish Government (”the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant and Global A.Ş. appealed the judgment of 7 November 2001. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment on 10 October 2002. On 13 January 2003 the applicant requested rectification of the Court ofCassation’s decision of 10 October 2001. On 11 April 2003 the court dismissed the applicant's request. The applicant was ordered to pay her TRL 1,512,000,000 with simple interest. The case was settled out of court in October 2004. The judge ruled in favour of the applicant and ordered the defendants to pay back the money. The appeal was dismissed on 11 April 2006. The decision was appealed by the applicant on 13 January 2007. The Appeal Court ruled in favor of the applicants.

name: Józef Kuśmierek
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr Józef Kuśmierek. name: George Runkee
train_texts: Cases originated in two applications (nos. 42949/98 and 53134/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants complained that, as men, they were not entitled to receive widows' benefits, including Widow's Pension, equivalent to those available to comparable bereaved women. By decisions dated 7 June 2001 and 4 April 2002, respectively, the Court declared the applications admissible. On 18 May 2005 the Court invited the parties to submit observations on the merits, but the Court decided that it would not be necessary. The applications were adjourned pending the conclusion of related domestic proceedings (see paragraphs 22-24 below) Mr White is a United Kingdom national, born in 1942 and living in Warrington. He and his wife had two children, one of whom was adopted and born in 1955. On 8 March 1999 his wife died. She had worked until the birth of her son in 1968 and had made reduced social security contributions. Mr White notified the Benefits Agency of his wife's death and of his intention to claim “widowers' benefits” on 10 March 1999. On 21 June and 8 September 1999, Angela Eagle, a Minister from the Department of Social Security, wrote to the applicant's Member of Parliament confirming that as a man he was not entitled to claim widows' benefits.

name: Roy H.W. Johnston
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9697/82) against Ireland lodged with the Commission in 1982 under Article 25 (art. 25) by Roy H.W. Johnston, an Irish citizen, Janice Williams-Johnston, a British citizen, and Nessa Williams-johnston, their daughter. The request sought a decision from the Court as to the existence of violations of Articles 8, 9, 12 and 13. The Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, having been informed by the Registrar of their right to intervene, did not indicate any intention of so doing. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. B. Walsh, the elected judge of Irish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. R. Ryssdal, the President. On 24 January 1986, the Chamber decided under Rule 50 to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The President directed on 30 January that the oral proceedings should open on 23 June 1986. The hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Gleeson and Mr. O’Reilly for the Government, by. Gaukur Jörundsson for the Commission and by Senator. Robinson and Dr. Duncan for the applicants. There appeared before the Court: Mrs. Liddy, Deputy Legal Adviser, Department of Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr. D. G. Lagergren, F. Gölcüklü and R. Macdonald (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21. 43). The case was heard by the High Court and the European Court of Human Rights. The case was brought by the Government at the request of the President of the Court and one of its members. The Court ruled in favour of the first applicant, who had been separated from his wife for more than 20 years. The second applicant, with whom Roy Johnston had been living since 1971, gave birth to his daughter in 1978. The first applicant is unable to obtain, in Ireland, a dissolution of his marriage to enable him to marry the second applicant. He has taken the following steps to regularise his relationship with her and with his wife and make proper provision for his dependents. The parties also mutually renounced their succession rights over each other’s estates. The third applicant has, under Irish law, the legal situation of an illegitimate child. Her parents are concerned at the lack of any means by which she can be recognised as their child with full rights of support and succession in relation to them. They are also concerned about the possibility of a stigma attaching to her by virtue of her legal situation, especially when she is attending school. The first and second applicants state that although they have not practised any formal religion for some time, they have recently joined the Religious Society of Friends (the Quakers) in Dublin.

name: David Adetoro
train_texts: The applicant alleged that he did not have a fair trial as a result of the trial judge's misdirection to the jury. The evidence against the applicant was almost entirely circumstantial and the case relied heavily on evidence from a police surveillance exercise carried out over a period of about one year. The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1972 and is currently detained in HMP Whitemoor, Cambridgeshire. He denied any involvement in the conspiracy to rob and was interviewed under caution in March and June 1997. The prosecution case was that the applicant joined the conspiracy in around April 1996 after his release from prison. The applicant pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to rob and other offences arising out of the conspiracy. During the interviews, he was asked to give an explanation for his movements as recorded by the police, his association with a variety of individuals and his whereabouts at the time of the robberies. On each occasion, he replied “no comment’. The judge directed the jury as to the burden of proof and the standard of proof in the case: “...The burden [of proof] lies upon the prosecution throughout the case, to prove their case against the defendant. The defendant does not have to prove anything at all, there is no burden upon him to proveanything” The judge noted that the applicant had not answered questions put to him during the police interviews, replying ‘no comment’ to each of the questions posed. The applicant did not suggest that he was advised by his lawyer not to comment but said that he did not want to incriminate people in relation to stolen vehicles. He admits that he failed to mention any of the facts to which I have just referred, when he was interviewed and he says his reason for that, was that although well knowing that others had been arrested for the much more serious offence of armed robbery, as he had been, he didn't want to incriminate them in the stealing of cars. On 18 June 1998 the jury found the applicant guilty of the offences charged. He was sentenced to 26 years' imprisonment. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal arguing, inter alia, that the summing up contained a Lucas direction (a direction to the jury in relation to lies – see paragraph 33) The judge was not prepared to place reliance on anything he said and made no finding in respect of Mr Shearer and Mr Stephenson’s presence or absence in the circumstances of the sixth robbery. The judge noted that he was satisfied that Mr Adetoro was involved in the sixth robber and ignored his assertion that he had been with them at the time. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed. However, his sentence was reduced to 22 years' imprisonment. The Court of Appeal disagreed and found that, despite the misdirection by the trial judge, the conviction was safe. It distinguished between cases where an accused exercised his right to silence pursuant to legal advice or because he was tired or ill and those where, as in the present case, the reason for not answering questions was linked to the fact that he had no answer that would hold up to scrutiny. The main ground of appeal was that the direction on adverse inferences was defective in that the jury were not directed that an adverse inference could only be drawn where it was satisfied that the real reason for the applicant's silence was that he has no answer to the questions asked. The court found that the jury had rejected the applicant's defence and, in doing so, must also have rejected his explanation of why he failed to answer questions in the police interview. The court also noted that the judge had given the jury an unnecessary Lucas direction which, in the event, provided assistance to the jury in how to approach the question of adverse inferences. name: İlhami Erseven
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 27225/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were members of the executive and auditors boards of the Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association (“the Association”), a non‑governmental organisation with its headquarters in Ankara. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the alleged breach of the applicants' right to a fair hearing to the Government. The Ankara public prosecutor imposed a fine of 92,510,0000 Turkish Turkish. On 15 January 2001 a payment order was served on the members of the executive and auditors boards who, however, did not pay the fine within the statutory ten-day time-limit. On 11 September 2001 the Ankara Magistrates' Court found the applicants and the other co-accused guilty as charged and sentenced them to an increased fine of TRL 136,890,0000 per person. In their petitions, the applicants maintained that they had been deprived of the opportunity to make defence submissions and that, therefore, they did not receive a fair trial. The Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance (asliye ceza mahkemesi) dismissed the applicants' objections on the following dates.
